display.prose: The query asks whether 'it is not the case that Ada has fur' follows from the premises. Consider how the only route to Ada having fur actually operates. The sole premise that mentions fur is p1: if Ada wears an amber pin, then Ada has fur. No premise states outright that Ada has fur. No premise states outright that Ada wears any pin, hat, or scarf. The twenty-two Ben register entries (p0, p3, p5–p8, p11–p14, p16, p17, p20, p21, p24–p31) concern only Ben's clerical records. They say nothing about Ada's body or clothing. Several register predicates share color words with Ada's garments: amber entries appear in registers 0, 8 and 16, scarlet in 7 and 15, and cobalt in 1, 9 and 17. These look connected to Ada's amber pin, scarlet hat and cobalt scarf, but the vocabulary keeps them as separate predicates. Recording an amber entry is not wearing an amber pin. The fact that the problem stacks so many colour-matched register facts, all about Ben, suggests the premises dwell on Ben's paperwork rather than on Ada's features. On the Ada side, the premise set is a chain of conditionals. Each one only passes along a hypothetical, from salmon to bird to flying and on through the clothing items. Since fur enters only as the final consequent of a conditional, the premises never place fur on Ada as a standalone fact. On this reading, the statement that Ada lacks fur is the conclusion the premise set supports, and the answer is True.
